meeting_header: Date: 2026-06-20 15:30 UTC | Duration: 78m | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Eli (Redwood SE), Priya (AegisMed Lead ML), Mark (AegisMed Infra), Daniel (AegisMed Compliance)
summary: Deep technical triage focused on accuracy regressions seen after mixed precision (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ) conversion in AegisMed's on‑prem deployment. Discussed KV cache staleness causing apparent hallucination/regression signals, batching window latency vs throughput tradeoffs, and a bisect/playbook approach for isolating per‑layer errors and sticky cache behaviors. Agreed next steps include deterministic bench runs, KV debug runtime, and follow‑up triage meeting.
topics: Quantization tradeoffs: INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ
KV cache behavior and staleness (sticky KV entries)
Batching windows: latency SLOs vs throughput targets
On‑prem network constraints and VPC peering implications
Bisecting for post‑quantize accuracy drops and fallback strategies
questions: Is the regression correlated with long context lengths or specific prompt prefixes?
Are drops happening deterministically for specific layers or inputs?
How does KV cache eviction interact with batching coalescing in our runtime?
Do we have audit/compliance constraints that prevent full logs export?
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): All right folks, thanks for joining. We're 78 minutes, agenda: dig into the post‑quantization accuracy drop you reported and run through a bisect/playbook. Eli will drive the stack traces.
[00:12] Priya (AegisMed): Thanks, yeah we've seen a consistent ~3‑6% drop on rouge/qa pass rates after converting to INT8/GPTQ mix. On‑prem only, not in cloud dev.
[00:25] Eli (Redwood): OK, that's helpful. Quick qualifier — are you using persistent KV cache across requests or a fresh cache per session?
[00:37] Mark (AegisMed): We shard KV cache across workers, we keep sticky prefixes for active sessions — so persistent across multi‑turns. We wanted throughput gains.
[00:48] Eli (Redwood): That tells me two things: one, sticky KV entries can interact badly with layerwise quantized kernels if caching assumes exact numerical reproducibility; two, batching windows plus cache coalescing can produce non‑deterministic ordering under load.
[01:02] Priya: When we downgraded from FP16 to INT8 some examples started hallucinating more, especially long context clinical notes. But it's intermittent — not always reproducible.
[01:15] Daniel (AegisMed, Compliance): Quick compliance note — we can only share de‑identified logs; anything with PHI needs redaction, we've prepared an obfuscated sample.
[01:25] Sofia: Perfect. We'll work with obfuscated logs. First hypothesis: quantization introduces small numeric shifts layerwise, and cached KV fragments preserve an earlier numerical state that isn't compatible after partial layer fallback or kernel substitution. That mismatch can amplify down the stack.
[01:40] Eli: To expand: AWQ/GPTQ do per‑layer statistics and sometimes store scale factors that assume specific kernel ordering. If runtime falls back a layer (say due to memory or precision gating), the cached keys signed with the previous representation can become 'stale' — the model sees inconsistent KV inputs.
[01:56] Mark: Hmm we did enable the runtime's precision gating heuristics to avoid large lat spikes. Could that be the trigger?
[02:05] Eli: Yes — precision gating is a double‑edged sword. It reduces tail latency by falling back to higher precision for problematic ops, but if you mix representations in a persistent cache without an invalidation strategy, you can create a semantic mismatch.
[02:20] Priya: So what's best practice for on‑prem: disable sticky KV? Force cache invalidation on rollout? Add cache versioning?
[02:30] Sofia: All options are valid depending on your SLOs. We recommended earlier: add cache versioning and include a quantization schema identifier in the KV metadata. That way, when you roll a quantized build, stale entries are ignored.
[02:45] Eli: Also we can enable per‑layer fallback masking — keep most layers INT8 but force critical layers (we found earlier it's often the first few attention layers) to FP16. That reduces regression risk but costs some perf.
[03:01] Priya: Are there rules of thumb for which layers to keep in FP16? In our models the top‑3 attention layers seem sensitive.
[03:12] Eli: Exactly — start with the first N attention layers and last M layers around the output projection. We also recommend a small eval set to validate. We'll share a script.
[03:25] Mark: Network note — our on‑prem infra has 25 Gbps interconnect between boxes but we saw jitter under load. Could jitter amplify batching reorder and worsen cache staleness?
[03:36] Eli: Definitely. Batching coalescing waits for a window; jitter can change which requests are coalesced together, altering the sequence of KV writes vs reads. If some replicas see write A then read B, others vice versa, sticky KV semantics are effectively non‑deterministic.
[03:52] Priya: That would explain intermittent behavior.
[03:55] Sofia: Let's map a concrete bisect plan: 1) deterministic bench across quantization schemes with fixed seeds and single‑threaded worker to remove jitter; 2) side‑by‑side runs with and without KV persistence; 3) controlled enabling of precision gating per layer; 4) check trace logs for KV version mismatches.
[04:14] Eli: For step 1 we'll provide a bench harness that runs AWQ, GPTQ, INT8, FP8 variants with 3 seeds and reports token‑level diffs and perplexity deltas. We want to isolate whether the accuracy drop is quantization‑type specific or an artifact of caching/batching.
[04:30] Mark: On the runtime side, can you add a flag to emit KV cache keys + schema id? Right now logs already have some hashes but not schema.
[04:40] Eli: Yes — we'll build a debug runtime with --kv-debug and --kv-schema flags; it'll tag entries with quant schema and timestamp. It will slow perf but good for triage.
[04:50] Priya: Will that run on our air‑gapped environment? We can't pull debug builds from public network.
[04:58] Sofia: We'll provide a signed binary and checksums through your S3 bucket; Daniel can verify signatures.
[05:06] Daniel: Good, make sure the binary passes our compliance checklist. We'll scan for unnecessary telemetry.
[05:12] Eli: The debug runtime will have a toggle to avoid external telemetry. It only writes to local logs you can bundle.
[05:20] Priya: Back to quant types — we saw AWQ gave better perplexity than GPTQ on our sample, but AWQ also increased tail latency. Is that typical?
[05:29] Eli: AWQ tries to preserve some distributional stats and often yields better accuracy for some LLM families, at a moderate perf cost. GPTQ can be faster but more brittle on some layers. FP8 is promising but hardware support on your on‑prem GPUs may be limited — you mentioned older Ampere cards?
[05:43] Mark: We're on A100 40GB, not the newest. FP8 paths may not be fully optimized.
[05:49] Eli: Right — A100 supports some FP8 kernels with mixed support across runtimes. Our runtime falls back to emulated FP8 or to INT8, depending on kernel availability. That fallback path is another possible source of variance.
[06:03] Priya: So we have three moving parts: quant scheme (AWQ/GPTQ/INT8/FP8), runtime kernel availability & fallbacks, and KV/batching interactions.
[06:13] Sofia: Correct. Hence the bisect: hold two constant, vary the third. Example matrix: fixed runtime (no fallback) + vary quant; fixed quant + vary cache persistence; fixed quant & cache + vary batching windows.
[06:26] Eli: Also add a deterministic sequence length sweep — the problem seems worse at >2K tokens in your initial report.
[06:36] Priya: Yes it's most pronounced at 2k–4k.
[06:39] Mark: Actionable asks from infra: can we pin scheduling so coalescing windows are consistent? We use a custom scheduler.
[06:47] Eli: You can try a fixed small window (e.g., 5ms) to reduce reorder, but that reduces throughput. There's always the latency/throughput tradeoff. We'll provide some throughput curves from our previous runs.
[06:58] Priya: How about cache eviction — should we evict on model rollout? We do nightly model swaps.
[07:05] Sofia: Ideally yes. Include a cache schema version and bump it on rollout. For fast rollouts you can also do a selective eviction for active sessions. Another approach: namespace the KV keys by quant schema so new schema reads won't pick older keys.
[07:19] Daniel: Any SOC2 or audit considerations if we add schema ids to KV keys? Could that leak config info?
[07:27] Sofia: The schema id is just an opaque hash. No config leakage. But if you prefer, you can HMAC the id with a per‑deployment secret.
[07:36] Mark: Network again — for on‑prem peering we saw occasional half‑opened sockets under heavy load. Could that cause partial KV writes?
[07:44] Eli: If a write isn't fully flushed and another request reads the partial entry, you can get corrupt keys. Our runtime has write‑atomicity guarantees but if OS level sockets drop you can see it. We should check logs for partial write retries.
[07:56] Priya: What's the quickest mitigation to reduce customer visible regressions while we triage?
[08:03] Eli: Quick mitigations: 1) disable sticky KV (make cache ephemeral per session) which reduces some perf but avoids stale mismatches; 2) force critical layers to FP16; 3) bump batching window to be deterministic. Any one reduces risk.
[08:18] Sofia: We also recommend a canary rollout with traffic mirror to a non‑sticky KV config to compare live.
[08:26] Priya: We can do a canary. Priya: (laughs) — sorry, me again — what's the expected perf hit for making layer 1–3 FP16?
[08:34] Eli: Depends on model size. For 30B models you might see 10–18% drop in throughput but smaller latency change. We'll provide numbers.
[08:45] Sofia: Let's talk instrumentation. We'll need token‑level diffs, per‑layer activations (or checksums), and KV schema tags. If we can reproduce, we may do a layerwise bisect: quantize up to Lx and run test; repeat to find the earliest layer with a reproducible drop.
[09:05] Mark: Can Redwood's runtime produce layer checksums without exposing activations? Compliance will prefer checksums over raw activations.
[09:13] Eli: Yes — we can emit SHA256 checksums of layer activations on CPU, not the raw tensors. That lets you verify mismatch points.
[09:22] Priya: Nice. What about stochastic rounding in quantization? I've read it can reduce bias but introduce run‑to‑run variance.
[09:31] Eli: Correct. Stochastic rounding reduces systematic quantization bias but increases nondeterminism; for benching we force deterministic rounding. For production you choose between lower bias or deterministic outputs.
[09:44] Priya: So bench runs use deterministic rounding and single worker to control variance. Got it.
[09:51] Sofia: We'll summarize the action plan: Redwood provides bench harness + debug runtime; AegisMed supplies obfuscated logs and prompt sets; run matrix and reconvene.
[10:02] Daniel: One small ask — include a short security note documenting what the debug runtime logs, so our security team can sign off.
[10:10] Sofia: We'll attach a one‑page doc.
[10:14] Eli: On a lower level — if we find a layer with reproducible drop with INT8 but not with AWQ, we'll try per‑layer AWQ patches or mixed precision for that subset. If that's not feasible, fallback policy: route critical traffic to dedicated FP16 nodes.
[10:30] Priya: That sounds reasonable if it's a small subset of requests.
[10:35] Mark: Curious — any prior examples where sticky KV was the root cause?
[10:40] Eli: Yes, a previous customer had persistent KV + mixed‑precision fallback and saw similar intermittent hallucinations. Fix was to include quant schema in KV and evict on rollout.
[10:50] Priya: Good to know.
[10:52] Sofia: Anything else we should cover?
[10:55] Mark: One question: will this triage require us to run on a single GPU for determinism? We normally use 4 per node.
[11:03] Eli: For the bench runs, single‑worker single‑GPU is best to remove multi‑worker nondeterminism. Once we have a repro we can scale to multi‑GPU to validate impact.
[11:12] Priya: Ok we can stand up a single‑GPU node.
[11:16] Sofia: Great. We'll aim to deliver the debug build and bench harness by 2026‑06‑24, template spreadsheet by 06‑22. Follow‑up meeting tentatively 2026‑06‑29.
[11:28] Daniel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:31] Sofia: Thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes / Imperfect transcriptions: sometimes "K V cache" appears as "K‑V cache" or "K B cache" in logs; some proper nouns may be garbled (A100 vs A‑100). Occasional filler "uh" and overlap between Priya and Mark.
